transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-02-14
Start: 10:30 UTC
Duration: ~58m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Price (Redwood SE), Liam O'Neill (Aperture Head of ML), Priya Rao (Platform), Marco Diaz (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
- Reviewed last week's baseline vs Redwood pilot benchmarks (p50/p95 latency, throughput RPS)
- Discussed enabling quantized model + routing to cheaper slots; initial unit cost looks promising but p95 spikes remain
- Agreed next steps: run KV cache prewarm, overnight 2hr load test with routing policy, share detailed logs and pricing

Topics:
- Latency distribution (p50/p90/p95), tail spikes during long seqs
- Throughput scaling with continuous batching and dedicated slots
- Quantization tradeoffs (8-bit vs 4-bit), slight rouge/ hallucination risk observed by customer on edge cases
- Routing & fallback policies when dedicated capacity is saturated

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining on a valentine's day bench scrub, appreciate it. quick check — everyone see the lab deck i dropped?
[00:12] Liam (Aperture): yep, saw it. skimmed. thanks maya. apologies, busy week so high level first then dive in.
[00:21] Jordan (Redwood SE): morning. i'll open with the updated numbers — we ran the quantized 8-bit build and the 4-bit alpha for the critical model.
[00:31] Priya (Aperture): quick Q — which quant library did you use? i saw notes referencing 'qkern' but our infra expects the open-q libs.
[00:41] Jordan: good call — we used Redwood internal compiles that pick kernels from qkern/oq depending on seq length. sometimes the transcript says 'q kern', 
[00:49] Marco (SRE): ok, baseline recap — our incumbent (CloudGen) p95 is ~860ms on 1k token runs at their provisioned slot; your hosted was showing 720ms p95 in last run?
[01:02] Jordan: right, the 8-bit on our dedicated pool hit p50 ~110ms, p95 ~410ms for 512 tokens in the midday profile. the 4-bit alpha reduces cost by ~37% but p95 bumps to ~560ms in one noisy run.
[01:18] Liam: those look good on paper, are we seeing tail spikes when seqs exceed 1k? that's our main concern — many inference calls bleed into 1.2-1.6k tokens because of medical notes.
[01:30] Jordan: yes, we did a long-seq stress. for 1.2k tokens the p95 went to ~780ms on 8-bit and 1.05s on 4-bit in the noisy iteration. but the key is KV cache hit ratio — when prefix-cache hits are high the tail is much better.
[01:46] Priya: wait — can you explain the KV cash — i mean KV cache prewarm step again, we heard 'KV cash' from earlier notes —
[01:53] Jordan: ha, yes 'KV cash' in the transcript. we prewarm the KV cache with representative prefixes so the model doesn't have to recompute early KV windows. that reduces token generation time for long continuing sessions.
[02:05] Marco: our current pipeline doesn't do prewarm; most of our calls are cold. that explains some of the CloudGen vs Redwood delta maybe.
[02:12] Maya: practical ask — if Aperture can replicate a high cache-hit workload, the p95 delta should be more pronounced in Redwood's favor. otherwise you're comparing cold start heavy mixes which favor the incumbent.
[02:24] Liam: got it. last week we ran a 30-minute run that was mostly cold; we can flip to 2 hours overnight with prewarm and share logs.
[02:32] Jordan: perfect. we also tried continuous batching enabled on the dedicated pool — that gave a 22% throughput bump at the same latency SLO for short responses (<256 tokens).
[02:42] Priya: the throughput numbers in the deck show 180 RPS at 256 token median, and your sheet shows 240 RPS with batching. can you reconcile?
[02:50] Jordan: the 180 RPS was on single-slot reserved capacity with conservative autoscale. 240 RPS was on a burst-binded run where we allowed 2 extra dedicated GPUs for 10 minutes. we should mark those differences; the deck note is a little ambiguous.
[03:03] Maya: noted — we'll update the deck to label burst vs steady-state.
[03:08] Liam: what about unit cost? right now CloudGen bill us ~0.018 per call unit (their calculation), your numbers suggest lower, but end-of-day we need to see per-1M token cost including tail retries and fallbacks.
[03:20] Jordan: preliminary unit cost delta: 8-bit quantized reduces cost by ~28% vs our non-quant baseline; when combined with caching and batching we project a 38-42% lower per-token unit vs CloudGen assuming 70% cache hit. but if your workload is mostly cold, realized savings will be closer to 10-15%.
[03:38] Marco: hmm, that math's important. can we see a cost sensitivity table that varies cache hit 20/50/80% and seq length buckets?
[03:47] Maya: yes — jordan will push that sensitivity table to the shared spreadsheet.
[03:52] Jordan: yep, i'll include p50/p95 latencies per cell as well.
[03:58] Priya: any notes on correctness/QA when you push 4-bit builds? we ran a small eval set and noticed a couple more hallucination-ish outputs for certain clinical abbreviations.
[04:10] Jordan: good to flag. 4-bit is aggressive and we saw distributional drift in specific tokens — mostly punctuation and rare entity normalization. we recommend running the eval prompts you use in prod against the quantized build; that's why we asked for the prompt set last week.
[04:24] Liam: we sent a 750 prompt eval set; did you run that?
[04:29] Jordan: we did an initial pass — 4-bit had +1.8% failure on canonicalization, 8-bit was within 0.2% of baseline. i'll attach the eval CSV to the ticket.
[04:40] Marco: routing concerns — what happens if dedicated pool saturates during a spike? do we overflow to a cheaper hosted tier or to a smaller model? what's the outage/fallback playbook
[04:51] Maya: our recommended fallback is first to fallback to a compatible smaller quantized variant (same model family) in the same region, then to cross-region fallback if policy allows. we can also set a rate-limit degradation path that returns truncated responses with a short error header rather than failing full.
[05:08] Priya: is there telemetry hooks we can attach? we need trace-level logs to show failovers for SRE/Compliance.
[05:15] Jordan: yes, we can push per-request routing events and model variant tags into your tracing pipeline. prepping the sample tracing config is on my list.
[05:23] Maya: note — some customers prefer a strict no-fallback policy (security), in which case we recommend reserving extra dedicated capacity with guaranteed slots.
[05:33] Liam: what about the dedicated slot cost to achieve our 99p95 target?
[05:37] Jordan: for your current traffic and the 1k token profile, our model suggests 4 dedicated slots with conservative headroom. that meets p95 ~430ms steady-state. to avoid fallback during spikes you'd want 6 slots. i'll include both options in the pricing attachment.
[05:52] Marco: can you explain the kernel selection comment in the notes — 'compiled kernel change for long seqs improved memory locality' — that sounded a bit magic.
[05:59] Jordan: sure — our compile phase can select between different attention kernels depending on seq length and hardware. for long sequences we pick a memory-optimized kernel which reduces memory copies and improves throughput at the cost of slightly higher per-token compute. it explains why dedicated long-seq runs improved by 12% after a kernel switch.
[06:18] Priya: will enabling that kernel require anything from our side?
[06:21] Jordan: no infra change; it's runtime compile choice. it may slightly alter latency distribution so we recommend re-running your evaluation suite.
[06:29] Liam: you mentioned a noisy run earlier where p95 increased for 4-bit — do you think that's hardware saturation or model quantization instability?
[06:36] Jordan: initial investigation shows it was a mixture: a burst of synthetic traffic coinciding with a cache cold start. we saw CPU queuing on the network side as well — so it's partially infra and partially quantization edge-case.
[06:48] Maya: on the security front, priya had a question last call about KMS integration and audit logs for private deploy — need to confirm where that stands.
[06:56] Priya: yes, we need HSM/KMS options; your shared security pkg mentions KMS but not HSM. also retention windows on logs for 13 months, and SSO integration notes.
[07:06] Jordan: we have HSM integrations in Private deployments and KMS in Hosted; i'll surface the Private deployment doc and a summary of audit retention settings.
[07:15] Marco: we'll review that with security. could you also add a sample SP-initiated SAML flow diagram?
[07:22] Maya: will do — i'll include that in the follow-up.
[07:27] Liam: ok, to recap what we need from Redwood: detailed sensitivity cost table varying cache hit and seq length, quantized eval CSVs, updated deck clarifying burst vs steady, sample tracing config, and pricing for 4 vs 6 dedicated slots.
[07:40] Jordan: yep, plus we'll push the kernel/compile notes and the 4-bit failure cases annotated.
[07:46] Priya: aperture action items — we'll run the overnight 2hr run with prewarm and post full telemetry, and provision VPC peering.
[07:55] Marco: also tagging our SRE lead for the next security session.
[08:00] Maya: sweet. any blockers before we close?
[08:04] Liam: just curiosity — are you seeing any real customers turning 4-bit on in prod?
[08:10] Jordan: a few early adopters but mostly in non-regulated verticals; in regulated health some customers prefer 8-bit for now and use 4-bit in canary.
[08:20] Maya: okay, we'll be judicious. thanks all — i'll follow up with the pricing and schedule the security deep-dive once you've had a look at the SOC2 packet.
[08:30] Liam: thanks, bye.

End of meeting.

Notes about transcript quality: occasional word swaps (KV cash, q kern), a few overlapping talk markers lost, speaker labels are mostly correct but may be off in short interjections.
